claims.text: Inspection: visual inspection is the central evaluation tool; many skin disorders are diagnosed by the appearance or morphology of the lesions, which may vary across different skin tones.
claims.quote: Visual inspection is the central evaluation tool; many skin disorders are diagnosed by the characteristic appearance or morphology of the lesions (see also Description of Skin Lesions), which may vary across different skin tones.

claims.text: Full skin exam: includes the scalp, nails and mucous membranes; it screens for skin cancers and looks for clues to the diagnosis of a widespread eruption.
claims.quote: A full skin examination, including examination of the scalp, nails, and mucous membranes, is done to screen for skin cancers and to detect clues for the diagnosis of a widespread eruption.

claims.text: Tools: a hand lens shows morphologic detail; a hand-held dermatoscope with built-in lighting is particularly useful for evaluating lesions; diascopy or a Wood light can add information.
claims.quote: Magnification with a hand lens can help reveal morphologic detail. A hand-held dermatoscope with built-in lighting is particularly useful in evaluating lesions. Further information can be gathered by using diascopy or a Wood light.

claims.text: Describe each lesion by: lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, location and distribution, and color.
claims.quote: An extensive language has been developed to standardize the description of skin lesions, including: Lesion type (sometimes called primary morphology) Lesion configuration (sometimes called secondary morphology) Texture Location and distribution Color

claims.text: Macule: flat, nonpalpable change in color, usually < 10 mm; not raised or depressed (eg, freckles, flat moles).
claims.quote: Macules are flat, nonpalpable lesions usually < 10 mm in diameter. Macules represent a change in color and are not raised or depressed compared to the skin surface. Examples of macules include freckles and flat moles.

claims.text: Patch: a large macule, usually > 10 mm (eg, vitiligo, port-wine stains).
claims.quote: Patches are large macules usually > 10 mm in diameter. They are not raised or depressed compared to the skin surface. Examples of conditions that may present with patches include vitiligo, pityriasis alba, and port-wine stains.

claims.text: Papule: elevated, palpable lesion, usually < 10 mm.
claims.quote: Papules are elevated lesions usually < 10 mm in diameter that can be felt or palpated.

claims.text: Plaque: palpable lesion > 10 mm, elevated or depressed compared to the skin surface (eg, psoriasis).
claims.quote: Plaques are palpable lesions > 10 mm in diameter that are elevated or depressed compared to the skin surface. Plaques may be flat topped or rounded or may be comprised of multiple groups of small papules. Lesions of psoriasis and granuloma annulare commonly form plaques.

claims.text: Nodule: firm papule or lesion that extends into the dermis or subcutaneous tissue (eg, cysts, lipomas).
claims.quote: Nodules are firm papules or lesions that extend into the dermis or subcutaneous tissue. Examples include cysts, lipomas, fibromas, and infectious conditions (eg, parapoxvirus lesions, sporotrichosis).

claims.text: Vesicle: small fluid-filled blister < 10 mm (eg, herpes infections).
claims.quote: Vesicles are small, fluid-filled blisters < 10 mm in diameter. Vesicles are characteristic of herpes infections, acute allergic contact dermatitis, and some autoimmune bullous disorders (eg, dermatitis herpetiformis).

claims.text: Bulla: fluid-filled blister > 10 mm.
claims.quote: Bullae are fluid-filled blisters > 10 mm in diameter.

claims.text: Pustule: a vesicle that contains pus.
claims.quote: Pustules are vesicles that contain pus.

claims.text: Wheal (urticaria): elevated lesion from localized edema, typically pruritic and erythematous; in dark skin tones erythema may be less visible, so look for edema or a surface or texture change.
claims.quote: Urticaria (wheals or hives) is characterized by elevated lesions caused by localized edema. Wheals may appear as localized lesions or as a more generalized eruption. Wheals are typically pruritic and erythematous; however, in patients with a dark skin tone, erythema may be less visible, and wheals may instead be identified by edema or by surface or texture change.

claims.text: Petechiae: nonblanchable punctate foci of hemorrhage.
claims.quote: Petechiae are nonblanchable punctate foci of hemorrhage.

claims.text: Purpura: larger area of hemorrhage that does not blanch and may be palpable; palpable purpura is the hallmark of leukocytoclastic vasculitis; large areas may be called ecchymoses.
claims.quote: Purpura is a larger area of hemorrhage that may be palpable. Purpura does not blanch. Palpable purpura is considered the hallmark of leukocytoclastic vasculitis. Purpura may indicate a coagulopathy. Small areas of purpura are called petechiae. Large areas of purpura may be called ecchymoses.

claims.text: Annular: rings with central clearing (eg, granuloma annulare, tinea, secondary syphilis).
claims.quote: Annular lesions are rings with central clearing. Examples include granuloma annulare, some drug eruptions, some dermatophyte infections (eg, tinea [ringworm]), and secondary syphilis.

claims.text: Target: rings with central duskiness; classic for erythema multiforme.
claims.quote: Target (bull’s-eye or iris) lesions appear as rings with central duskiness and are classic for erythema multiforme.

claims.text: Lichenification: thickened skin with accentuated skin markings, from repeated scratching or rubbing (eg, atopic dermatitis).
claims.quote: Lichenification is thickening of the skin with accentuation of normal skin markings; it results from repeated scratching or rubbing and is commonly seen in chronic inflammatory dermatoses (eg, atopic dermatitis).

claims.text: Induration: deep thickening of the skin with a hard, resistant feel, from edema, inflammation or infiltration, including by cancer.
claims.quote: Induration, or deep thickening of the skin, can result from edema, inflammation, or infiltration, including by cancer. Indurated skin has a hard, resistant feeling.

claims.text: Distribution — note whether: lesions are single or multiple; particular body parts are affected (eg, palms or soles, scalp, mucosal membranes); the distribution is random or patterned, symmetric or asymmetric; lesions are on sun-exposed or protected skin.
claims.quote: When examining the skin, it is important for clinicians to note whether: Lesions are single or multiple. Particular body parts are affected (eg, palms or soles, scalp, mucosal membranes). Distribution is random or patterned, symmetric or asymmetric. Lesions are on sun-exposed or protected skin.
claims.locator: Location and Distribution of Skin Lesions

claims.text: Color and skin tone: a patient's skin tone can affect the coloring of lesions and other skin signs.
claims.quote: When examining the color of skin, health care professionals should note that a patient's skin tone can impact the coloring of lesions and other skin signs.

claims.text: Yellow skin: typical of jaundice; in dark skin tones, scleral icterus and mucosal surfaces may give clearer contrast.
claims.quote: Yellow skin is typical of jaundice, xanthelasmas and xanthomas, and pseudoxanthoma elasticum. In patients with a dark skin tone, scleral icterus and mucosal surfaces may provide clearer diagnostic contrast.

claims.text: Nikolsky sign: epidermal shearing with gentle lateral pressure on seemingly uninvolved skin (toxic epidermal necrolysis, some autoimmune bullous diseases).
claims.quote: Nikolsky sign is epidermal shearing that occurs with gentle lateral pressure on seemingly uninvolved skin in patients with toxic epidermal necrolysis and some autoimmune bullous diseases.
claims.locator: Other Clinical Signs of Skin Lesions

claims.text: Auspitz sign: pinpoint bleeding after scale is removed from psoriasis plaques.
claims.quote: Auspitz sign is the appearance of pinpoint bleeding after scale is removed from plaques in psoriasis.
claims.locator: Other Clinical Signs of Skin Lesions

claims.text: Koebner phenomenon: new lesions within areas of trauma (eg, scratching, rubbing, injury); frequent in psoriasis, also lichen planus.
claims.quote: Koebner phenomenon describes the development of lesions within areas of trauma (eg, caused by scratching, rubbing, or injury). Psoriasis frequently exhibits this phenomenon, as may lichen planus, often resulting in linear lesions.
claims.locator: Other Clinical Signs of Skin Lesions

claims.text: Darier sign: rapid swelling of a lesion when stroked (urticaria pigmentosa, mastocytosis).
claims.quote: Darier sign refers to rapid swelling of a lesion when stroked. It occurs in patients with urticaria pigmentosa or mastocytosis.
claims.locator: Other Clinical Signs of Skin Lesions

claims.text: Dermatographism: an urticarial wheal where focal pressure is applied (eg, stroking or scratching the skin).
claims.quote: It is the appearance of an urticarial wheal after the application of focal pressure (eg, stroking or scratching the skin) in the distribution of the pressure.
claims.locator: Other Clinical Signs of Skin Lesions
